notes.meaning: Pashhur was an important priest in charge of temple security. When he heard Jeremiah warning the people about coming destruction, he grew very angry. Instead of listening to God's message, this religious leader decided to silence the prophet.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentators note that temple officers had a duty to stop false prophets, and Pashhur treated Jeremiah as an impostor.

notes.meaning: Pashhur ordered Jeremiah to be beaten and locked in the stocks. The stocks twisted the prisoner's body into a painful and unnatural position. By placing him at the Upper Gate of Benjamin, Pashhur made sure everyone passing the temple could see and mock him.

The next day, Pashhur released Jeremiah from the painful frame. Jeremiah did not keep quiet out of fear, but immediately gave Pashhur a new name from God: Magor-missabib. This name means 'terror on every side,' showing that panic would soon surround the priest.

The Lord told Pashhur that his false sense of safety was over. He would become a terrifying sight to himself and to the friends who trusted his lies. Soon, the army of Babylon would take Judah captive and kill many people before his eyes.

God announced that all the wealth of Jerusalem would be handed over to the invaders. Everything the people had worked for and all the royal treasures would be carted away to Babylon. Trusting in money and city defenses could not protect them once God withdrew His care.

Pashhur learned that his high office would not save him from exile. He, his family, and his supporters would be dragged off to Babylon. He would die there as a captive because he had promised peace when God had decreed judgment.

Jeremiah poured out his personal pain to God after his release. He felt overwhelmed by the prophetic calling that God had pressed upon him. Instead of being honored, he faced constant ridicule and shame every single day.

differ.view: Calvin taught that Jeremiah spoke ironically, echoing his mockers to show that their insults were really aimed at God Himself.
John Gill explained the phrase as God powerfully persuading Jeremiah to serve, while also seeing a struggle between human weakness and spiritual faith.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentators noted that God never promised Jeremiah a life without pain, but simply withheld how hard the path would be.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Modern translations often render the opening words to say God coerced or overpowered Jeremiah into taking up the role of prophet.

notes.meaning: Every time the prophet opened his mouth, he had to warn the people about oncoming violence and disaster. The people did not want to hear about their sins, so they laughed at his warnings. Doing what God asked brought him nothing but public contempt.

Jeremiah decided in his heart that he would stop preaching and stay quiet. Yet God's message became like a blazing fire trapped deep inside his bones. He tried to hold it back, but the Lord's calling was too powerful to suppress.

Jeremiah heard crowds plotting against him and whispering hostile threats. Even close acquaintances watched him closely, hoping he would slip up and make a mistake. They wanted an excuse to arrest him and get revenge for his hard sermons.

Suddenly Jeremiah remembered who was on his side. The Lord stood with him like a mighty warrior, far stronger than any human enemy. Because God was his defender, his persecutors would eventually fail and suffer everlasting disgrace.

Jeremiah placed his whole case before the Lord of hosts, who sees every secret thought and motive. Instead of seeking personal payback, he trusted God to bring about true justice. Leaving vengeance to God brought peace to the prophet's troubled mind.

Faith lifted Jeremiah out of deep distress into a song of joyful praise. He called on everyone to thank the Lord for rescuing poor and defenseless people from cruel bullies. Even while danger remained, he knew God had already secured the final victory.

The chapter shifts abruptly to an agonizing cry as Jeremiah curses the day he was born. After his bold faith, the raw memory of his deep suffering broke through again. His extreme grief shows how painful his ministry felt in moments of exhaustion.

differ.view: Calvin held that Jeremiah was recalling his past thoughts during the stocks to show how low he had sunk before God lifted him up, while still viewing the curse as a serious fault.
John Gill saw this sudden lament as an example of human weakness, impatient flesh, and momentary lack of faith overcoming a godly man.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentators understand this language as poetic imagery describing intense suffering rather than actual sinful despair.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Modern scholars view these verses as personal lament poetry without claim to divine revelation, noting strong literary parallels with Job's speeches.

notes.meaning: Jeremiah went on to curse the messenger who brought his father the happy news of his birth. A baby boy was usually a cause for great celebration in an ancient family. Yet Jeremiah felt so crushed by his life's mission that he wished no one had ever rejoiced.

Jeremiah wished that the messenger had shared the total ruin of Sodom and Gomorrah. He described a life filled with constant alarms, waking up to panicked shouts in the morning and war cries at noon. The heavy poetry shows how endless his own terror felt.

In his bitter sorrow, Jeremiah wondered why he had not died before he ever took a breath. He wished his mother's womb had been his grave so that he never had to live in such pain. The words reflect the desperate feelings of an honest sufferer wrestling with his grief.

The chapter closes with a heart-wrenching question about why he had been born at all. It seemed to Jeremiah that his whole life had produced only hard labor, deep sorrow, and public disgrace. Even in his darkest grief, he directed his honest complaints to God rather than walking away from Him.
